title: New insights for composition design: A novel synergistic corrosion-resistant effect of Fe–Mn–Al–Cr–Si–Mo–C lightweight steel in 3.5 wt% NaCl solution
abstract: Nowadays, a good corrosion resistance of lightweight steel is demanded for its application. However, due to the high contents of Mn and C, which are always corrosion-susceptible elements in steels, the conventional lightweight steel is not desirable for this mission. Although Cr is widely believed to be a common alloying element to improve the corrosion resistance of most steels, it is considered to be ineligible using in the lightweight steel due to the relatively high content of C. This is because the trade-off between corrosion resistance and mechanical properties by alloying Cr. In recent years, the rapid developments of additive and coating manufacturing have provided new possibilities for both the Cr alloying and microstructural modulation to improve corrosion resistance of lightweight steel. In this case, to design a certain chemical composition using in additive and coating manufacturing, it is interesting to clarify the effects of Cr alloying on the corrosion resistance of lightweight steel. To reveal it, in the present work, the Fe–Mn–Al–Cr–Si–Mo–C lightweight steel alloyed with Cr contents of 4 wt%, 8 wt% and 12 wt% are prepared. The corrosion resistances and mechanisms of Cr-alloyed lightweight steels in 3.5 wt% NaCl solution are investigated by electrochemical and immersion tests. The present work may provide new insights for the composition design of lightweight steel, especially for the directions of additive and coating manufacturing.
journal: Journal of Materials Research and Technology

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Since the Fe–Mn–Al–C steels exhibit a yield strength of 0.4–0.9 GPa, an ultimate tensile strength of 0.6–2.0 GPa, an elongation of 30%–80%, and a density of 6.5–6.8 g cm −3  [ 1–5 ], it is considered to use in broad prospects such as navigation, automotive and aerospace due to their excellent mechanical properties and low density [ 6–10 ]. The current application of Fe–Mn–Al–C alloy shows a growing demand for good corrosion resistance, especially for applications used in acidic and alkaline environments as well as environments containing halogen elements [ 11–13 ]. However, the Fe–Mn–Al–C steel shows relatively poor corrosion resistance due to the intergranular corrosion along the duplex-phase boundary [ 14–16 ], and the formation of detrimental κ-carbide [ 14 , 17 ] as well as the MnO and MnO 2  among the corroded surface as a result of a high content Mn [ 18 ].

The addition of corrosion-resistant element is a useful approach to improve the corrosion resistance of alloyed steel, which can form a dense passivation layer to hinder the entry of corrosive elements into the matrix. For example, Zhang et al. [ 19 ] and Yang et al. [ 20 , 21 ] have confirmed that the additions of Ca, Sb, and Te in lightweight steels can significantly improve their corrosion resistances under different environments. Specifically, Ca can improve the corrosion resistance of steel by modifying the harmful MnS inclusion into the favorable MnS–CaAl 2 O 4  inclusion. While Sb can enhance the consumption of H +  to reduce the electrochemical activity on surface. Additionally, Te can reduce pitting corrosion and inclusions-induced corrosion. Besides, various corrosion-resistant elements can generate a synergistic effect and remarkably enhance the corrosion resistance of alloyed steels. For example, Mo, Cr, and Ni are all corrosion-resistant elements used in stainless steel. Among them, Cr prone to segregated at grain boundary in the form of carbide, hence inhibit intergranular corrosion. It also can significantly enhance the resistance against pitting corrosion by the formation of a passivation layer on the surface [ 22–24 ]. In terms of Mo, it can form various oxides combined with oxides of Cr and Ni to form a passivation layer of complex compounds on the matrix's surface in steel alloy, thus further enhancing the corrosion resistance [ 25–27 ]. For the lightweight elements, Al and Si can play positive roles in improving the corrosion resistance. The former one can produce a dense Al 2 O 3  passivation film on the surface during the corrosion process [ 28 , 29 ]. The later one can interact with FeOOH and other corrosive elements, which increases the density of oxide at surface and thus enhances the corrosion resistance [ 30 ]. Besides, Lai et al. [ 31 , 32 ] have reported that the Si addition can effectively improve the steel's mechanical properties by inhibiting the formation of brittle martensitic phase and hydrogen-enhanced intergranular crack due to the increase of stacking fault energy (SFE). Therefore, Si is a prospective alternative lightweight element candidate for lightweight steel owing to both its effect on corrosion and mechanical properties.

For the lightweight steel, one of the advantages is its low cost, since most alloyed elements in the lightweight steel (C, Mn and Al) are relatively cheap. Besides, recent studies show that the individual additions of Cr, Mo, and Ni into the lightweight steels can enhance their corrosion resistances [ 13 , 33 , 34 ]. To design a lightweight steel with both low cost and considerable corrosion-resistant proprieties, the corrosion resistance and mechanism of lightweight steel with comparable low Cr contents are of great interest. According to the studies of stainless steel [ 35 , 36 ], when the mass fraction of Cr in the steel is higher than 12%, the corrosion resistance can be remarkably improved as a result of dense passivation layer on the matrix's surface. However, although Cr is widely believed to be a common alloying element to improve the corrosion resistance of steels, this is not a consensus for the lightweight steel due to the relatively high content of C [ 17 , 23–25 , 33 , 34 , 37 ]. Specifically, in the conventional casting methods, when the Cr content is higher than about 4 wt% in the lightweight steel, the formation of Cr-rich carbide along grain boundary leads to the degradation of mechanical properties. Whereas, undesirable corrosion resistance is found in the lightweight steel with Cr content less than 4 wt%. This means a trade-off between corrosion resistance and mechanical properties by Cr alloying. Consequently, Cr is considered to be ineligible using in the lightweight steel. In recent years, the rapid developments of additive and coating manufacturing have provided new possibilities for both the Cr alloying and microstructural modulation to improve corrosion resistance of lightweight steel. For the additive and coating manufacturing, since they experience different process and show different microstructural modulation, more attention is focused on the effect Cr addition on the corrosion resistance of lightweight steel in spite of possible weakness of mechanical properties. Based on the knowledge of above studies, in the present work, a Fe–Mn–Al–Cr–Si–Mo–C lightweight steel is designed to explore the possible solution of improving the corrosion resistance. Among the corrosion-resistant elements of this designed lightweight steel, the corrosion behaviors of Cr and Al may be the most interesting issues, which play the primary roles in the corrosion mechanisms of stainless steels and Fe–Mn–Al–C lightweight steels, respectively. For the stainless steels, dense Cr 2 O 3  and CrOOH passivation films are responsible for their excellent resistant properties [ 38 ]. Whereas Al 2 O 3  passivation films are reported to enhace the resistant properties of lightweight steels to some extent [ 1 , 39 ]. However, the combination effects of several corrosion-resistant elements on the corrosion resistances and mechanisms of lightweight steel is still an open question.

Additionally, although it seems that conducting direct experiments by additive and coating manufacturing to design a certain chemical composition is reasonable, the complicated parameters of additive and coating manufacturing themselves always leads to uncertain results of both microstructure and corrosion resistance. For example, to determine a certain additive manufacturing process, numerous parameters need to be set including laser power, scanning speed, spot diameter, layer thickness, particle sphericity and size distribution, scanning pattern, building orientation, hatch distance and gas atmosphere. These parameters remarkably affect both the microstructure and building defects such as porosity, keyhole and lack-of-fusion, which may cause uncertainty of corrosion resistance. In contrast, the specimen of as-cast state by conventional casting may provide much more stable and repeatable results far beyond those by additive and coating manufacturing. To investigate the feasibility of composition design in this study, the as-cast ingots with different Cr contents up to 12 wt% were prepared and used as the subject material due to their stable and repeatable experimental results. The effects of Cr contents on the corrosion resistance of prepared steel in sodium chloride solution were revealed by electrochemical and immersion tests. The corrosion resistances and mechanisms were investigated through electrochemical tests, including open circuit potential (OCP), potentiodynamic polarization (PDP) and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS), which were analyzed based on the characterizations of microstructure and element distribution of as-cast specimen as well as the morphology and corrosion product of corroded surface after immersion tests. The present results may provide a glance about the roles of Cr in the corrosion behaviors of lightweight steels to some extent, which may be useful for estimating the effects of Cr contents on their corrosion resistances and helpful for the composition design of lightweight steel, especially for the directions of additive and coating manufacturing.

sections.heading: Materials
paragraphs:
In this study, lightweight steel alloys with Cr contents of 4 wt%, 8 wt%, and 12 wt% were fabricated by smelting and casting at vacuum, respectively. The lightweight steel ingots are prepared by a vacuum melting furnace belonging to the HBIS GroupCo., Ltd. Mo is often added together with Cr and can enhance the ability to resist pitting and intergullar corrosion. Meanwhile, the addition of B can play a role in partially replacing corrosion-resistant elements such as Ni, Cr, and Mo, and further strengthen the corrosion resistance [ 40 , 41 ]. Thus, these elements were also alloyed in steels. The chemical compositions of as-cast ingots are shown in  Table 1 
                         , which were tested using an inductively coupled plasma atomic emission spectrometry (ICP-AES, Agilent 5110, Agilent Technologies). According to their Cr contents, these specimens were designated as 4Cr, 8Cr, and 12Cr, respectively. The sizes of ingots were 150 × 150 × 180 mm, as shown in the supplemented material S1. All the specimens in this study were obtained in the equiaxed-grain zone, where the sampling positions were 30 mm away from the surfaces of ingots. In this case, all the specimens were isotropic. Optical microscopy (OM) was used for specimens observation.

sections.heading: Microstructural characterization
paragraphs: The phases information of steel were analyzed by an X-ray diffraction (XRD, Aeris, Malvern Panalytical) using a Cu radiation (Ka = 0.154 nm), working with parameters of a tube voltage of 30 KV, a scanning rate of 2°/min, a step size of 0.05°, and a 2θ from 30° to 90°. The specimens for XRD analyses were cleaned by ethanol after grinding sequentially by SiC sandpaper from 200# to 2000#. The microstructural and corrosion morphologies as well as element distributions were detected by an electron probe x-ray microanalyzer (EPMA, EPMA-1720 Series, SHIMADU) and a scanning electron microscopy (SEM, Sigma 300, ZEISS) equipped with an energy dispersive spectrometer (EDS, Aztec, Oxford instruments). The volume fractions, element distributions, and compositions of different phases were determined by EPMA mapping and Imaging Pro Plus software.

The specimens for microstructural morphologies were mechanically grounded sequentially by SiC abrasive papers from 200 # to 3000 #, and then polished by diamond suspension with particle size from 7 to 1.5 μm. The polished surfaces were etched using a 4 wt% nitric acid-alcohol solution before inspection.

sections.heading: Electrochemical test
paragraphs:
Electrochemical tests including OCP, PDP, and EIS were carried out at ambient temperature (25 ± 1 °C) by an electrochemical workstation (CHI650E, CH instrument) in 3.5 wt% NaCl solution. The schematic diagram of experimental setup is shown in  Fig. 1 
                         . A three-electrode system was used, where the reference electrode (RE) was a saturated calomel electrode (SCE) with saturated KCl, the counter electrode (CE) was a pure Pt (99.9%Pt) electrode, and the specimen was immersed as a working electrode (WE). By embedding specimens (10 × 10 × 2 mm) in epoxy resin, a surface with a dimension of 10 × 10 mm 2  is exposed, which is connected to the electrochemical workstation by a copper conductor. To remove the oxide on the surface and to ensure the post-polished working surface, the specimen was mechanically grounded by SiC sandpapers from 200 # to 2000 #.

Depth, size, and distribution of corrosion pits and products on the surface were observed using a three-dimensional profilometry (UP-Dule, Rtec instruments). The resolution of depth/height measurement is 0.14 nm, while the resolution of horizontal measurement is 0.5 μm. Based on the three-dimensional (3D) morphology data, analysis of corrosion pits and corrosion products were carried out by MountainsMap software.

Corrosion product analysis was analyzed using an X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS, Thermo Scientific K-Alpha, Thermo Fisher), whose parameters were an excitation source of Al-Kalpha (h v  = 1486.3 eV), a pressure of less than 2.0 × 10 −7  mbar, a spot size of 400 μm, an operating voltage of 12 kV, a filament current of 6 mA, a full-spectrum scanning fluence of 150 eV in steps of 1 eV, and a narrow-spectrum scanning fluence of 50 eV in steps of 0.1 eV. The dimension of specimen was 5 × 5 × 3 mm, which was immersed in 3.5 wt% NaCl solution for 10 days.

sections.heading: Microstructure
paragraphs:
The microstructural morphologies and XRD patterns of as-cast Fe–Mn–Al–Cr–Si–Mo–C alloys with varied Cr contents are shown in  Figs. 2 and 3 
                         
                         . For the 4Cr specimen, the matrix primarily consists of γ-austenite and δ-ferrite, where the δ islands are surrounded by the γ phase. Whereas the matrixes of 8Cr and 12Cr specimens are single ferrite phase due to the increase of Cr content (ferrite stabilizing element). Moreover, combined with the results by XRD and OM, the average grain sizes of specimens increase with the elevation of Cr content. Besides, due to the exitence of duplex-phases, the average grain size of 4Cr specimen is much finer compared with the other ones. Additionally, since all the specimens are cooled slowly in the furnace, numerous reticulated distributed precipitates along the boundaries are identified, which are also detected by the XRD patterns. While few precipitates are observed in the grain interiors. Among them, only a small amount of fine precipitates was generated in the 4Cr specimen, which were distributed along the boundaries of duplex-phases. In contrast, both the amounts and size of precipitates in the 8Cr and 12Cr specimens increase significantly compared with that of 4Cr specimen, whose volume fractions seem to reach saturation with the elevation of Cr content. The chemical compositions and volume fractions of precipitates along the grain boundaries of different steels will be analyzed in the following contexts.

The element distributions of three steels are shown in  Fig. 4 
                          and  Table 2 
                         . As regards the matrix of 4Cr, the volume fractions of δ and γ phases are 54.99% and 38.76%, respectively. The contents of primary elements in the δ and γ phases are different, i.e. Si, Al, Cr and Mo are favorable to segregate in ferrite phase, while C, Mn and Ni are segregated in austenite phase. Notably, among all the three steels, most element contents in the δ phase change slightly except for Cr, which will be discussed later combined with the content variations of precipitates. In terms of precipitates along the grain boundaries, as shown in  Fig. 4  and  Table 2 , they are alloyed carbides composed of C, Cr, Mn, Fe and Mo. Among them, the contents of C, Cr and Mo in the precipitates are much higher than those in the matrix, i.e. the precipitates are Cr–Mo-rich carbides. Additionally, the volume fractions of Cr–Mo-rich carbide in the 8Cr and 12Cr exhibit remarkable increases compared with that of 4Cr one. However, the values between the 8Cr and 12Cr are almost equivalent, which indicates that the volume fraction of Cr–Mo-rich carbide approaches saturation when the addition of Cr content is larger than 8 wt%.

Compared with the element distributions between the matrix and carbide, although the Cr content increases remarkably in both the matrix and carbide from the 4Cr to 12Cr, their Cr content variations show different tendencies at the critical value of 8 wt%. When the Cr content is less than 8 wt%, the Cr addition leads to the coarseness of Cr–Mo-rich carbides and the increase of precipitate's volume fraction due to the Cr segregation along the grain boundary in advance. On the contrary, if the Cr content was larger than 8 wt%, the volume fraction of Cr–Mo-rich carbides reached saturation and the Cr content doped into the matrix increases dramatically. These differences may significantly affect the corrosion properties of Fe–Mn–Al–Cr–Si–Mo–C alloys, which will be discussed in the following chapters.

sections.heading: Electrochemical test result
paragraphs: The corrosion properties of as-cast specimens in 3.5 wt% NaCl solution are characterized by the standard electrochemical tests, including OCP, PDP, and EIS, which indicates that the corrosion resistance of specimen in 3.5 wt% NaCl solution increases significantly with the elevation of Cr content, especially for the specimen with a Cr content beyond 8 wt%

Fig. 5 
                         a shows the open-circuit potentials of specimens in 3.5 wt% NaCl solution. The potentials of 4Cr and 8Cr are relatively stable, with values of −409 and −416 mV, respectively. For the 12Cr, the potential initially becomes more negative with the increase of test time, however, it eventually approaches a constant value of −401 mV. It may be attributed to the formation of high-density Cr-rich oxides on the surface of 12Cr at the early corrosion stage, which gradually detach and shift the potential toward more negative values during the further corrosion process.  Fig. 5 b and  Table 3 
                          show the PDP curves of specimens and the analyzed parameters of these curves. During anodic polarization, the 12Cr appears a visible platform of polarization current density with the increase of polarization voltage, which is not observed in the curves of 4Cr and 8Cr specimens. This indicates that the 12Cr specimen exhibits a remarkable passivation behavior during the corrosion process [ 24 ]. In this case, the corrosion properties of 12Cr specimen during anodic polarization should be described by the passivation potential (E p ) and the dimensional passivation current density (I dp ), which are −0.33 V and 0.66 μA/cm 2 , respectively. However, in terms of 4Cr and 8Cr specimens, since they do not appear obvious passivation behavior, their corrosion properties should be described by the corrosion current density (I corr ) and polarization resistance (R p ), whose values are calculated using Eq.  (1) . As shown in  Table 3 , relatively large I corr  and low R p  are found in the 4Cr and 8Cr specimens. On the contrary, favorable I dp  value of 0.66 μA cm −2  and R p  value of 31.91 kΩ cm 2  are obtained in the 12Cr specimen, which indicates a desirable resistance against corrosion in 3.5 wt% NaCl solution. Notably, these values obtained in the 12Cr specimen improves dramatically than those of Fe–25Mn-2.7Al–4Cr-0.2Si-0.3C steel and Fe–30Mn-3.1Al-1.4Si-0.05C duplex-phase steel, whose values are 8.51 μA cm −2  and 29.00 μA cm −2 , respectively [ 12 , 33 ].

As shown in  Fig. 5 (e) and (f), two types of fitting circuits are adopted to investigate the corrosion impedances of specimens according to their corrosion behaviors. For the 4Cr and 8Cr specimens, a semicircle is shown in the Nyquist curve and a single peak is exhibited in the Bode plot, which indicates a none-passivation behavior. However, for the 12Cr specimen, the Nyquist curve shows a visible plateau and the Bode plot exhibits two peaks, which demonstrates a passivation behavior. Besides, the same phenomenon can be also found in the polarization curves of specimens. Consequently, the R (QR) fitting circuit is suitable for the 4Cr and 8Cr specimens, while it is more reasonable to use the R (Q (R (QR))) fitting circuit for the 12Cr specimen [ 18 ].

Additional information is provided by vis-à-vis Nyquist and Bode plots to illustrate the corrosion resistance of specimens based on the EIS test results, as shown in  Fig. 5 c and d, respectively. Besides, the schematic diagram of electrical equivalent circuit (ECC) used to fit the EIS test results is also plotted in  Fig. 5 e and f, which includes solution resistance (R s ), film resistance (R film ), charge transfer resistance (R ct ), and film capacitance (CPE film ), double layer capacitance (CPE dl ). The capacitive reactance arcs are observed in both the high- and low-frequency regions. The fitting parameters of EIS tests are listed in  Table 4 
                         . At low frequency (<10 Hz), both the Nyquist and Bode plots illustrate that the impedance of specimen in 3.5 wt% NaCl solution improves remarkably with the elevation of Cr content. For example, both the capacitive reactance arcs in  Fig. 5 c and the impedance modulus in  Fig. 5 d demonstrate that the corrosion resistance of specimen in 3.5 wt% NaCl solution increases significantly with the elevation of Cr content, especially for the specimen with a Cr content beyond 8 wt%. Moreover, the R ct  value of 12Cr specimen is 21.23 kΩ cm 2 , which also indicates a favorable resistance to corrosion in 3.5 wt% NaCl solution and is much better than those of Fe–30Mn–10Al–2Mo-1.2C light-weight steel and Fe–20Mn-9.1Al-0.8C-4.5Ni steel, whose values are 6.67 kΩ cm 2  and 5.50 kΩ cm 2 , respectively [ 25 , 47 ].

sections.heading: Weight loss and corrosion rate
paragraphs:
Fig. 6 
                             shows the corrosion rate (V corr ) of specimens immersed in 3.5 wt% NaCl solution for 4, 7, and 10 d. The values of V corr  are calculated using Eq.  (2) . The V corr  of specimens reduce remarkably with the elevation of Cr content, especially for specimens with a Cr content beyond 8 wt%. This tendency is the same as the results obtained in the electrochemical test. Both the results obtained in the electrochemical and immersion tests indicate that the addition of Cr content is an available approach to improve the corrosion resistance of Fe–Mn–Al–C lightweight steel in 3.5 wt% NaCl solution. Besides, the V corr  values of specimens reduce with the elongation of immersion time. These are supposed to correlate with the formations of protective passivation layers on the surface, which will be analyzed and discussed in the following context.

sections.heading: Macroscopic corrosion morphology
paragraphs:
Figs. 7–9 
                            
                            
                             shows the 3D corroded surface morphologies of steels immersed in 3.5 wt% NaCl solution for 4, 7, and 10 days. The average depth (D av ) of corrosion pits and average height (P av ) of corrosion product are given in  Table 5 
                            . The corrosion pit is always adjacent to the corrosion product. For example, local corrosion is observed on the surface of 12Cr specimen, where the vicinity of corrosion pits is surrounded by the corrosion products, while other surface areas are still smooth without severe corrosion, as shown in  Fig. 9 . This may be because the locally formed corrosion product disrupts the structural integrity of passivation layer on the surface of steels and changes the reaction potential between the interface and the solution, making it easier to form pit around the area with the accumulated corrosion product.

The corroded surface morphologies show remarkable differences based on the different Cr contents. The degrees of corrosion reduce with the elevation of Cr content, especially for the specimen with a Cr content of 12 wt%. For the 4Cr, obvious corrosion is found after immersion for only 4 days and an entire mess surface with plentiful corrosion products and corrosion pits is formed after immersion for 10 days. In contrast, scarcely any corrosion product or corrosion pit can be found in the 8Cr and 12Cr specimens after immersion for 4 days and only a spot of one is formed after immersion for 7 days. Among the 8Cr and 12Cr specimens, the areas of smooth surface without severe corrosion are different after immersion for 10 days, where about half of smooth area still exists in the 8Cr specimen, while the vast majority of surface in the 12Cr specimen is smooth one and only a few local accumulated agglomerations of corrosion products and corrosion pits appear.

The degrees of corrosion in the three steels are also supported by their D av  and P av , which appears to be consistent variations with the changes of corroded surface morphologies. Both the D av  and P av  increase steadily with the increase of immersion time in all the specimens, which are also demonstrated as the progressive corrosion processes as shown in  Figs. 7–9 . Interestingly, the variations of D av  and P av  increase dramatically while the V corr  decreases with the elongation of immersion time, which seems to show the opposite trend of their corrosion process. The reasons for this phenomenon are two-fold. Firstly, the V corr  is tested by the electrochemical test, which measures the actual corrosion rate of matrix and excludes most corrosion products on the surface. At same time, the D av  and P av  are tested by immersion test, which displays the information of both the matrix and residual corrosion products on the surface and definitely cannot serve as a parameter to characterize the degree of corrosion. Moreover, for example, when the immersion time is 10 days, as analyzed above, the D av  and P av  of 4Cr specimen are the average values measuring the entire mess surface with plentiful corrosion products and corrosion pits. However, the D av  and P av  of 4Cr specimen are the average values obtained from a few local accumulated agglomerations of corrosion products and corrosion pits, meanwhile most smooth areas do not contribute to the measurements of D av  and P av . Therefore, with the elongation of immersion time, although both the D av  and P av  of all specimens increase promptly, their V corr  decreases primarily due to the different corrosion behaviors between specimens with different Cr contents, which is supposed to correlate to the formations of protective passivation layers on the surface of specimens.

sections.heading: Corrosion morphology and product
paragraphs:
Fig. 10 
                             shows the corrosion morphologies on the surfaces of specimens at the initial state after 2 h of immersion corrosion. At the initial state, the corrosion occurs by pitting corrosion at the triple junction or quarter node of grain boundary or phase boundary between austenite and ferrite phases. Then, it corrodes into the grain interior and along the grain boundary due to intergranular corrosion. The sizes and depths of pits decrease with the elevation of Cr content in the specimens, indicating that the corrosion resistant increases with the elevation of Cr content. The massive precipitates with spherical or polyhedral morphologies imbedded in the pits are responsible for the preferential corrosion owing to the galvanic corrosion between the matrix and precipitates.

Figs. 11–13 
                            
                            
                             show the surface morphologies and the elemental distributions of steels after immersion for 10 days.  Fig. 11  shows that the corroded surface is composed of three different layers: the uppermost deposition, the secondary corroded film, and the matrix under them. In the deposition, a large number of spherical oxides and chlorides are accumulated on the surface of 4Cr specimen, which are determined to be a majority of Al 2 O 3  and a tiny number of oxides and chlorides with other corrosion-resistant elements, including Si, Cr and Mo. Besides, the corroded film beyond the matrix consists of primary Cr-rich chlorides. In this case, Al and Cr play an individual role in protecting the matrix from corrosion.

However, hardly any oxides or chlorides of corrosion-susceptible elements, such as Fe and Mn, are found in both the surface deposition and the corroded film. In contrast, Fe and Mn appear only in the matrix exposed to the coarse corrosion cracks and pits.

Regarding the 8Cr, its surface shows a similar morphology to that of 4Cr except for the remarkable refinement of crack dimension. However, the chemical compositions of both deposition and corroded film in the 8Cr are significantly different from the 4Cr. Not only the contents of corrosion-resistant elements, such as Cr and Mo, increase in the deposition and corroded film, but the corrosion-susceptible elements, such as Fe and Mn, are also retained in them. This indicates that the elevation of Cr content doped into the matrix can stabilize the corrosion products to form a hybrid compound and avoid detachment, especially for the corrosion products of Fe and Mn. In this case, Al, Cr and other corrosion-resistant elements generate a synergistic effect to protect the matrix from corrosion.

In terms of 12Cr specimen, although its surface also has a three-layer structure as those of 4Cr and 8Cr specimens, its morphology is essentially different from the others, which creates a smooth and dense corroded film without apparent crack and tip. Besides, its chemical compositions are almost equivalent to the matrix, indicating a favorable resistance against corrosion. Additionally, the deposition of 12Cr specimen is polyhedral and does not agglomerate together. Moreover, their chemical compositions also demonstrate that the high Cr and Al content doped into the matrix is available to form a hybrid compound and reinforce the other elements against corrosion and detachment, especially for the elements of Fe and Mn. In this case, the synergistic effect of corrosion-resistant elements is further improved due to both the high Cr and Al content doped into the matrix.

According to the above results, after immersion in 3.5 wt% NaCl solution for 10 days, all specimens exhibit a three-layer structure consisting of deposition, corroded film, and matrix. However, with the elevation of Cr contents, the corrosion products change gradually from a deposition of spherical Al 2 O 3  as well as a corroded film with a mass of cracks and pits deposition of polyhedral hybrid compound and a dense corroded film. The high Cr and Al content doped into the matrix generates synergistic effect with other corrosion-resistant elements against corrosion and remarkably suppresses the detachment of corrosion-susceptible elements such as Fe and Mn.

sections.heading: XPS test results
paragraphs:
Fig. 14 
                             shows the X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) results of corrosion products on the surface of three steels after immersion for 10 days. The corrosion products of all specimens are composed of not only elements such as Al, Si, Cr and Mo, which have inactive potentials to anti-corrosion reaction and improve corrosion resistance [ 23 , 24 , 29 , 30 ], but also elements such as Fe and Mn, whose corrosion products are always not stable and dense enough during corrosion [ 18 , 48 ]. Besides, the binding energy positions and peak shapes of corrosion products in all the specimens are almost identical, indicating no unexpected bond forms owing to the Cr addition. Specifically, the states of Fe 2+  (FeO, 708.1 eV), Fe 3+  (Fe 2 O 3 , 710.2 eV), Fe 3+  (FeOOH, 712.0 eV), Mn 2+  (MnO, 640.83 eV), Mn 4+  (MnO 2 , 642.23 eV), Al 3+  (Al 2 O 3 , 74.10 eV), Si 4+  (SiC, 100.60 eV), Si 4+  (SiO 2 , 103.40 eV), Cr 3+  (Cr 2 O 3 , 577.3 eV), Cr 3+  (CrOOH, 578.3 eV) and Mo 4+  (MoO 2 , 232.48 eV) and Mo 6+  (MoO 3 , 235.68 eV) can be identified in  Fig. 14 . Moreover, a variety of complex Si oxides is also observed in the Si 2p spectral peaks, which is demonstrated as the broad peaks ranged from 101.00 to 103.00 eV and hard to identify [ 49 ]. Additionally, some bonds of elementary substance, such as Si 0  (99.4 eV), Cr 0  (574.8 eV) and Mo 0  (231.01 eV), are found in the specimens, which are supposed to form temporarily at the beginning of corrosion due to their relatively high redox potentials to against corrosion reactions [ 30 , 50 , 51 ]. In contrast, since the corrosion-susceptible elements, such as Fe and Mn, as well as Al with a low redox potential (

                             = −1.66 V vs. SHE) react with O 2−  and Cl −  in advance during corrosion [ 18 , 52 ], no bond of elementary substance is found in  Fig. 14 .

Among all the elements, the variations of Al, Si and Mo are slight between the specimens with different Cr contents. However, the XPS of Fe, Mn and Cr exhibit remarkable differences in the intensities of bonds between the specimens with different Cr contents, which supports the corrosion resistances and corrosion product structures of specimens obtained in the above results. For the corrosion resistance, the valence state of element indicates the degree of corrosion to some extent [ 13 , 24 , 47 ]. For example, with the elevation of Cr content in the specimen, the peak intensity ratios of Fe 3+ /Fe 2+  are 36.75, 25.00 and 6.20, while the peak intensity ratios of Mn 4+ /Mn 2+  are 9.76, 3.43 and 0.92, respectively. These indicate that more severe oxidation occurs in the 4Cr specimen, which weakens with the addition of Cr, especially for the specimen with a Cr content beyond 8 wt%. Besides, the state of Cr 0  is detected in the 4Cr specimen, whereas no peak is found in the 8Cr and 12Cr specimens. This means when the Cr content of specimen is larger than 8 wt%, Cr may participate more intensively to form corrosion products against the corrosion. Both of them are consistent with the results of corrosion resistances and corrosion products in the specimens with different Cr contents.

Regarding the structure of corrosion product, the increase of hydroxide bonds, such as FeOOH and CrOOH, is responsible for the different structures in the 4Cr specimen and others. For example, both the intensities of FeOOH and CrOOH in the 8Cr and 12Cr specimens enhance significantly compared with that of 4Cr specimen. In this case, the hydration reactions bind compounds of different elements to form hybrid compounds, which are the corrosion products of 8Cr and 12Cr specimens detected by the EDS analyses.

sections.heading: Corrosion mechanisms
paragraphs:
According to the above results, the corrosion resistance of Fe–Mn–Al–Cr–Si–Mo–C specimen in 3.5 wt% NaCl solution improves remarkably with the elevation of Cr content, especially for the specimen with a Cr content beyond 8 wt%. Besides, the specimens with Cr contents beyond or below 8 wt% may exhibit different corrosion mechanisms. Additionally, although the formation of Cr–Mo-rich carbide along the grain boundary may suppress the intergranular corrosion of specimen to some extent, the Cr–Mo-rich carbide plays a trivial role in contributing to the corrosion resistance compared with the Cr content doped into the matrix. This is because the corrosion resistance improvement of specimen shows a positive correlation with the Cr content doped into the matrix. Still, it appears to have a weak relation with the volume fraction of Cr–Mo-rich carbide, as shown in  Table 6 
                         . When the Cr content of specimen increases from 4 wt% to 8 wt%, the volume fraction of Cr–Mo-rich carbide in the specimen increases remarkably, while the corrosion resistance only improves slightly. Besides, when the Cr content in the specimen is beyond 8 wt%, the volume fraction of Cr–Mo-rich carbide reaches saturation. However, the corrosion resistance increases dramatically with the further increase of Cr content. On the contrary, the variation tendencies between the corrosion resistance and the Cr content doped into the matrix are almost the same.

For the phase constituent, the 4Cr specimen is austenite-based duplex-phase steel while 8Cr and 12Cr specimens are δ-ferrite single-phase steel. Generally, the austenite phase is considered to be corroded seriously than ferrite phase in duplex-phase steel [ 1 , 53 ]. The dominant reason is that the austenite phase concentrates higher content of corrosion-susceptible elements such as C and Mn, while its corrosion-resistant elements including Cr, Mo, Al and Si are lower. However, in this study, the differences of corrosion resistance between austenite and ferrite phases are supposed to be weak for the following reasons. For the 4Cr specimen, as shown in  Table 2 , the composition differences between austenite and ferrite phases are relatively small. Besides, their crystal structure differences are also comparably slight. Thus, the corrosion resistances between them should not be significantly different. Additionally, indeed, the phase constituent can affect the corrosion resistance due to the phase boundary corrosion to some extent. Nevertheless, since the relatively small differences of composition and crystal structure between austenite and ferrite phases in the 4Cr specimen, the phase boundary should not be remarkably different from grain boundary. Therefore, it is considered that the phase constituent plays a secondary role in contribution to the corrosion-resistance.

The corrosion mechanisms of specimen with different Cr contents are illustrated in  Fig. 15 
                         . The corroded surface is composed of three different layers: the uppermost deposition, the secondary corroded film, and the matrix beneath them. When the specimen's Cr content is low (<8 wt% in the whole specimen or < 6 wt% in the matrix), the Cr addition leads to the preferential precipitates of Cr–Mo-rich carbide along the grain boundary due to the Cr segregation, while the Cr content doped into the matrix is low, as shown in  Fig. 4  and  Table 2 . In this case, the Cr is not so active in forming oxides, as evidenced by the Cr metallic bond detected in the 4Cr specimen. Besides, the Fe and Mn in the matrix are severely corroded to be compounds of Fe 3+  and Mn 4+  and detach easily from the surface, leaving a residual deposition of dominating spherical Al 2 O 3  and a non-dense corroded film with plentiful cracks and tips, as shown in  Figs. 11 and 15(a) . Although this kind of deposition and corroded film still shows moderate corrosion resistance, a mass of cracks and tips exists in the corroded film. It exposes the in-depth matrix as shown in  Figs. 7 and 11 , which causes the infiltration of O 2−  and Cl −  along corrosion pits and cracks, and further deteriorates the corrosion resistance. Therefore, the corrosion mechanisms of specimens with Cr content below 8 wt% are dominated by the persistent detachment of Fe and Mn corrosion products. The evolution process of non-dense corroded film through the formation and expansion of corrosion pits and cracks is both the result and the cause of Fe and Mn dissipation.

When the specimen's Cr content is high (>8 wt% in the whole specimen or > 6 wt% in the matrix), the Cr content doped into the matrix increases dramatically due to the saturated precipitates of Cr–Mo-rich carbide. In this case, Cr may participate intensively in corrosion reactions and reinforce the other elements to form hybrid compounds by hydration reactions as shown in  Figs. 13 and 14 . This indicates that Cr can generate a synergistic effect with other corrosion-resistant elements against corrosion and remarkably suppresses the dissipation of corrosion-susceptible elements such as Fe and Mn. As a result, the deposition of polyhedral hybrid compounds is observed in  Fig. 13 , which is different from the deposition's morphologies and chemical compositions in  Fig. 11 . Moreover, a dense passivation film forms beyond the matrix with only a few local corrosion pits, as shown in  Figs. 9, 13 and 15(b) . This passivation film retains Fe and Mn in the passivation film by reducing both the corrosion degree and detachment of their corrosion products, which are confirmed by the differences in Fe and Mn valence states as well as element distributions of corroded surfaces between the 4Cr and 12Cr specimens. Therefore, the corrosion mechanisms of specimens with Cr content beyond 8 wt% are governed by a novel synergistic effect of corrosion-resistant elements due to the formation of hybrid compounds and dense passivation films induced by the intensive reactions of Cr, which inhibits the corrosion of Fe and Mn by preventing the infiltration of O 2−  and Cl −  into the matrix. Notably, this synergistic corrosion-resistant effect induced by the corrosion reactions of Cr is different from those corrosion mechanisms of individual Cr 2 O 3  and CrOOH passivation film reported in stainless steel [ 40 ] or individual Al 2 O 3  passivation film reported in lightweight steel alloy [ 11 ]. Therefore, the designed lightweight steels in this study show improvements of corrosion properties compared with other Fe–Mn–Al–C lightweight steels, as shown in  Table 7 
                         . Since most steel alloys do not alloy with both the corrosion-resistant Cr and corrosion-susceptible Mn together, the synergistic corrosion-resistant effect found in this study may provide a new perspective to improve the corrosion resistance of Fe–Mn alloy.

sections.heading: Outlook
paragraphs: In the present work, the Fe–Mn–Al–Cr–Si–Mo–C alloy is found desirable for the application under a corrosion environment due to a reduced density and an enhancing corrosion resistance with the increase of Cr content doped into the matrix, especially for the Cr content of 12 wt%. The reason is found due to a novel synergistic effect induced by both the high Cr and Al contents. These findings are important to design a certain chemical composition using in additive and coating manufacturing. At present, further studies by the consequent process based on the as-cast lightweight steel have been carried out by the authors, and some breakthroughs have been already obtained due to this synergistic corrosion-resistant effect. This indicates that the works in this study may serve as a guidance of a promising direction in the future lightweight steel research.

sections.heading: Summary and conclusion
paragraphs:
In the present work, the effects of Cr contents on corrosion mechanisms in a novel Fe–Mn–Al–Cr–Si–Mo–C as-cast lightweight steel are investigated by electrochemical tests and immersion tests in 3.5 wt% NaCl solution. The following conclusions are obtained. 
                         
                            (1) 
                            As expected, the corrosion resistance of specimen increases with the elevation of matrix's Cr content, whereas the microstructure (phase or carbide) plays a trivial role in contributing to the corrosion resistance. However, unexpected and dramatic improvements of corrosion resistances occur in the specimens with Cr contents larger than 8 wt%. Moreover, numerous evident of passivation behavior is found in the specimen with Cr content of 12 wt%. 
                         
                         
                            (2) 
                            The formation of hybrid compounds and dense passivation films are found on the corroded surfaces of specimen with a high Cr and Al content, which is competently different from those corrosion mechanisms of stainless steel and conventional lightweight steel. 
                         
                         
                            (3) 
                            Induced by both the high Cr and Al contents of matrix, a novel synergistic effect of all corrosion-resistant elements (Al, Si, Cr, and Mo) is revealed through hydration reactions, which remarkably suppresses the dissipation of corrosion-susceptible elements such as Fe and Mn.
